Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: FinchAI x Redwood — Quantization Profiles POC scoping
Recorded: 2025-01-14 18:00 UTC
Duration: 52 min
Attendees:
- Markus Klein (Redwood) — Solutions Engineering
- Aditya Rao (Redwood) — Product (Optimize)
- Mateo Alvarez (Redwood) — Serving Runtime
- Jonas Weber (Redwood) — Evals/Perf
- Nina Patel (FinchAI) — Head of Platform
- Eric Huang (FinchAI) — Staff ML Engineer
- Sofia Reyes (FinchAI) — Eng Manager, Summarization

Auto-Summary (generated)
- FinchAI is looking for aggressive inference cost reduction for high-volume summarization workloads; target is 30–40% reduction without breaking output quality/formatting.
- Redwood walked through the opt-in Quantization Profile Library concept and emphasized route-level enablement, canary rollout, and fast rollback to baseline.
- Key risk areas called out by FinchAI: JSON-mode formatting stability, long-context performance, and avoiding noisy regressions that only show up on specific routes.
- Agreed POC should be limited to 1–2 routes first (batch summarization + optionally one low-risk internal endpoint), with explicit success criteria and monitoring.

Topics
- Current FinchAI workload shape (batch summarization vs interactive)
- What “route-scoped quantization” means in Redwood
- Quality gates (eval harness + prompt sets) and safe rollout/rollback
- Success metrics: cost per 1M tokens, p95 latency, 5xx rate, JSON validity
- Practical scoping: model candidates, hardware constraints, and timeline

Questions
- Can FinchAI opt-in only for background queues and leave interactive chat on baseline?
- How does Redwood handle hardware incompatibility (wrong GPU arch) or a bad profile?
- What signals can auto-disable quantization for a single route?
- Do we need a Dedicated cluster to get predictable economics?

Transcript

[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool, thanks everyone for hopping on. Goal today is to scope a POC around quantization profiles. I know you all have a pretty specific target on cost.

[00:12] Nina Patel: Yep. We’re basically trying to cut our spend in half, but realistically if you can get us like thirty, forty percent, we can make it work. We’re at… high volume summarization. Like, it’s just constant.

[00:27] Markus Klein: Got it. And you’re mostly using Redwood Hosted today or you’re on another provider?

[00:32] Nina Patel: We’re mixed. Some workloads are on a hosted provider, some are self-hosted with vLLM. The reason we’re talking is we don’t want to run the whole fleet ourselves.

[00:44] Aditya Rao: Makes sense. And just to anchor terms: what we’re rolling out is an opt-in “Quantization Profile Library.” Redwood publishes profiles per model, like fp16 vs int8 vs int4 variants, including hardware constraints and expected cost/latency deltas. Then you can enable those profiles per route.

[01:05] Sofia Reyes: When you say “route,” that’s like our summarization endpoint, not the model name, right?

[01:10] Aditya Rao: Exactly. Think “/v1/summarize” or whatever you’ve defined in Redwood as a route config. You can keep “/chat” baseline and only quantize background jobs.

[01:22] Eric Huang: Okay. Our big fear is we’ve done quantization before and quality regressions are not uniform. Like you’ll pass a generic eval, then the one route that does structured JSON starts producing slightly malformed stuff.

[01:36] Jonas Weber: Yeah, totally. That’s basically why we’re making it route-scoped and opt-in. We don’t assume it’s safe everywhere. For POC we’d want your representative prompt sets for the routes you care about, including JSON-mode or tool calling if that’s part of it.

[01:53] Nina Patel: We do both. We have one route that returns strict JSON. Another that’s “free form” summaries.

[02:01] Markus Klein: Great. It sounds like two routes right there: low risk (free-form) and high risk (strict JSON). For the POC, I’d recommend we start with the low-risk one, then optionally canary the JSON route if we have good validity checks.

[02:18] Sofia Reyes: What do you mean by “canary” in your system? Is that a percent traffic slider? Or do we have to do it via headers?

[02:27] Aditya Rao: For this feature we’re aiming for route-level controls in the console and API. Canary typically means “enable quantization for X% of requests on that route.” You can do 5%, then 25%, etc. No need to change app code in the ideal case.

[02:47] Eric Huang: That’s good. We tried header-based toggles with another vendor, and it got messy.

[02:54] Mateo Alvarez: Also, from runtime side, the request path will evaluate: do we have a compatible quant profile for this model and hardware; is it enabled for this route; and if anything doesn’t line up we fall back to baseline. We don’t hard fail the request for a profile mismatch.

[03:12] Nina Patel: So in a worst case it just runs slower and more expensive, but it works?

[03:17] Mateo Alvarez: That’s the goal, yes. There are edge cases like if a kernel is selected incorrectly, but we’re putting guardrails around “incompatibility means baseline,” plus metrics so we can see when fallback is happening.

[03:32] Markus Klein: Let’s back up a sec and get the shape of your workload. Roughly tokens per request and concurrency?

[03:38] Sofia Reyes: Summaries are usually 1,500 to 6,000 input tokens. Output maybe 200 to 600. For batch, concurrency is high but not interactive. For interactive chat, it’s like p95 matters.

[03:56] Nina Patel: We also have long context sometimes—like 12k, 16k. Not the majority, but it happens.

[04:03] Jonas Weber: That matters for quantization. Some profiles behave great on short context and then degrade on long context due to KV cache pressure, kernel choices, that kind of stuff.

[04:14] Eric Huang: Yeah. We saw that with int4. It’s cheap but long context got weird.

[04:21] Mateo Alvarez: And sometimes it’s not even “quality,” it’s perf regressions because attention kernels change. So for the POC we should define a few sequence length bins you care about.

[04:33] Markus Klein: Okay. If your target is 30–40% cost reduction: do you care if latency goes up slightly on batch? Or do you need latency flat?

[04:43] Nina Patel: For background summarization, we can tolerate slower as long as throughput is good. For interactive, we can’t take a big hit.

[04:53] Aditya Rao: Perfect use case for route-level policy. You can set “batch route: quantize with int8 or int4,” “interactive route: baseline or conservative int8 only.”

[05:05] Eric Huang: Do you support int4 right away? Or is that like “later?”

[05:11] Aditya Rao: Depends on model family and hardware. For some model families, int8 is our first safe bet. int4 can yield bigger savings but also higher risk. I’d propose POC targets int8 first, then stretch goal int4 if evals pass.

[05:28] Nina Patel: We want aggressive. But I hear you.

[05:31] Markus Klein: Aggressive but safe. Let’s talk success criteria so we’re aligned.

[05:36] Markus Klein: For cost: is it “cost per million tokens,” or total monthly spend, or something else?

[05:43] Nina Patel: We look at cost per million tokens by route. We also track cost per document summarized.

[05:50] Aditya Rao: Good. We can instrument execution mode tags, so you can see “quantized vs baseline” cost/latency. For POC we’ll measure savings on the route.

[06:02] Jonas Weber: For quality: do you already have automatic checks? Like ROUGE, factuality, format validators?

[06:09] Eric Huang: We have internal evals. Mostly LLM-as-judge plus some string checks. For JSON route we do strict schema validation.

[06:18] Jonas Weber: Great. For our gating, we’ll run baseline vs quantized on your prompt sets. We’ll report deltas and we’ll want an explicit threshold: like “no more than X% regression” on your judge score, and “JSON validity must remain above 99.5%” or whatever makes sense.

[06:35] Nina Patel: JSON validity is basically non-negotiable. If it drops even a little, our pipeline breaks.

[06:41] Mateo Alvarez: That suggests we should keep JSON route on baseline until we have a really solid profile and maybe we do canary with automatic rollback if validity dips.

[06:52] Sofia Reyes: Automatic rollback is key. We had an incident last year where some change caused 5xx and it took us hours to isolate.

[07:01] Markus Klein: On that: the system supports “disable quantization per route” quickly. For POC we can define rollback triggers: e.g., 5xx rate, p95 latency spike, JSON validity, and some quality score.

[07:15] Nina Patel: How fast can you disable? Like, is it instant?

[07:18] Aditya Rao: It’s configuration-driven; in practice it’s minutes, not hours. There’s also caching of profiles, but toggles are designed to propagate quickly.

[07:29] Mateo Alvarez: Right. Profiles themselves can be cached, but policy evaluation can be refreshed frequently. We also have a “flush cache” capability if a profile is bad.

[07:40] Eric Huang: I’m going to ask an annoying question: if a quantized profile is “mis-scoped” to the wrong GPU class, does it crash?

[07:49] Mateo Alvarez: Ideally it doesn’t. There are compatibility checks: GPU arch, kernel availability, runtime version. If mismatch, we fall back to baseline. You’ll see a metric like “quant_fallback_reason=hardware_mismatch.”

[08:04] Jonas Weber: And from publishing standpoint, profiles are scoped and validated per hardware. We don’t want a profile that claims it works on A10 and then actually doesn’t.

[08:13] Nina Patel: Okay.

[08:14] Markus Klein: Let’s talk deployment mode. Are you thinking Hosted API for the POC, or do you need Dedicated capacity?

[08:22] Nina Patel: For economics we might want Dedicated eventually. But for POC we can do Hosted if you can give us enough consistency to measure.

[08:31] Markus Klein: We can do Hosted with a stable configuration, but if you want very stable throughput we might reserve some capacity for the POC window. We can figure that out.

[08:43] Sofia Reyes: We also have data constraints. Nothing super regulated, but we do want some audit logs and we need to know prompts aren’t used for training.

[08:52] Markus Klein: Standard: we don’t train on customer data. For audit logs and RBAC, we can share docs. But today’s focus—POC scope—still good.

[09:02] Aditya Rao: On safety: the “opt-in” is deliberate. We don’t turn it on globally. You pick routes, you pick canary percentage, and you can set default fallback.

[09:13] Eric Huang: That’s the part we like. With Together we had to manage it mostly in our app logic.

[09:20] Markus Klein: Helpful context. Can you share which models you run today?

[09:24] Eric Huang: We’re mostly on Llama-based models. Also evaluating some other open weights. For summarization we’ve got a tuned variant.

[09:35] Mateo Alvarez: If it’s a fine-tuned variant, we’ll need to confirm we can apply a published quant profile safely. Some quantization is sensitive to calibration data.

[09:45] Eric Huang: We can provide calibration prompts if needed.

[09:48] Jonas Weber: Great. Usually we want a calibration set plus an eval set. And for long context, we want a small but representative sample.

[10:00] Nina Patel: Can we set this up so our background queue goes to a “quantized route” and everything else stays the same? Like no code changes, ideally.

[10:09] Aditya Rao: Yes, the intent is you keep the same route and flip a toggle. But sometimes teams choose to create a separate route like “/summarize_batch” vs “/summarize_interactive.” Up to you.

[10:21] Sofia Reyes: We already have separate endpoints in our gateway, so mapping to two Redwood routes is fine.

[10:28] Markus Klein: Perfect.

[10:30] Markus Klein: Let’s define POC timeline. Would a 2-week POC be enough?

[10:35] Nina Patel: If we can see data quickly, yes. We want to make a decision this quarter.

[10:42] Markus Klein: Okay. Proposed phases: week one—offline eval + perf sanity. Week two—canary on batch route, monitor, then expand.

[10:55] Jonas Weber: For offline eval we’ll need your prompt sets. Ideally 200–500 examples per route to start. If you have more, great, but we can start smaller.

[11:08] Eric Huang: We can do 300-ish for batch, 200 for JSON.

[11:14] Jonas Weber: That’s workable.

[11:17] Mateo Alvarez: And perf: we’ll run across your typical seq length distribution. We’ll look at p50/p95 latency and throughput. For batch we can also look at “tokens per second per GPU,” though in Hosted it’s a bit abstract.

[11:34] Nina Patel: The metric we care about is basically $/doc and throughput in docs per minute.

[11:40] Aditya Rao: We can map that using your average tokens/doc.

[11:46] Markus Klein: Let’s get specific on success criteria. Tell me if this is reasonable:
- Cost: >= 30% reduction on batch summarization route compared to baseline.
- Quality: no more than 1% regression on your internal judge score; JSON validity stays >= 99.9% on JSON route (if we test it).
- Reliability: no increase in 5xx above baseline + small epsilon, like 0.1% absolute.
- Latency: batch route can tolerate some increase, but interactive route stays within, say, 10% p95.

[12:19] Nina Patel: That sounds close. I’d say JSON validity has to be basically flat. And for batch, latency can go up, but we don’t want like 2x.

[12:30] Sofia Reyes: Yeah, if it doubles it’ll back up our queue.

[12:34] Mateo Alvarez: We can use a conservative profile first. int8 often gives you savings without crazy latency change. int4 sometimes changes the kernel path in a way that can be slower for some shapes.

[12:49] Eric Huang: Wait, int4 can be slower?

[12:51] Mateo Alvarez: Sometimes, depending on sequence length and whether the kernel is optimized. It’s not always “smaller is faster.”

[12:59] Eric Huang: That’s… good to know.

[13:02] Aditya Rao: And that’s why profiles include “expected speedup/cost delta” plus constraints. We don’t want folks guessing.

[13:12] Nina Patel: Okay. On rollout: can we do route-level canary by percent and also by customer? Like, we have some tenants that are more tolerant.

[13:22] Aditya Rao: We can discuss per-customer overrides. For POC, simplest is route-level canary. But yes, the control model supports multiple layers of policy.

[13:33] Sofia Reyes: If we do canary, can we pin the profile version? Like if you publish a new one mid-POC, we don’t want it changing.

[13:41] Jonas Weber: Yes. Profiles are versioned. You can pin to an id/version so it’s stable.

[13:48] Nina Patel: Great.

[13:50] Markus Klein: There’s also the question of “what happens if quality regression shows up only in production.” Do you have monitoring signals?

[13:58] Eric Huang: We can sample outputs and run validators. We already do that.

[14:03] Jonas Weber: Perfect. If you can feed us the pass/fail rate per route over time, we can use that as a rollback trigger.

[14:12] Mateo Alvarez: On our side, we can tag traces and metrics with the “quant profile id” and “execution mode.” So you can correlate a spike to a specific profile.

[14:25] Nina Patel: That’s important. We’ve had “mystery drift” where we couldn’t tell what changed.

[14:31] Aditya Rao: Exactly. We want a clean audit trail: who enabled it, what route, what percentage, and what profile version.

[14:42] Sofia Reyes: Speaking of: who is allowed to flip these toggles? We need RBAC.

[14:47] Markus Klein: Yeah. In console/API we enforce permissions. For POC we can restrict to your admin group.

[14:55] Nina Patel: Okay.

[15:00] Markus Klein: Let’s talk about the “aggressive cost reduction” ask. Realistically, int8 might get you 15–30% depending on model. int4 can get higher but higher risk. Does that still meet your needs?

[15:16] Nina Patel: If we get 25–30% and it’s safe, we can sell that internally. But we’ll want a path to more.

[15:24] Aditya Rao: That’s fair. We can frame POC as: phase 1 int8, prove safety and controls. Phase 2 int4 for the batch route only.

[15:35] Eric Huang: We’d do int4 only on batch, never interactive.

[15:39] Mateo Alvarez: That aligns with what we see.

[15:42] Jonas Weber: For int4, we’ll be more conservative on what we publish. It’ll require stronger eval coverage.

[15:50] Nina Patel: What’s your coverage right now? Like do you have prompt sets for summarization?

[15:55] Jonas Weber: We have general sets and some summarization. For your POC, your internal set will be the main gate.

[16:04] Markus Klein: Cool. Do you want us to run some of your traffic through canary and compare costs in real time? Or just do a controlled batch test?

[16:12] Nina Patel: Controlled first, then canary.

[16:15] Sofia Reyes: Yeah. We’d like to avoid surprises.

[16:19] Markus Klein: Great.

[16:21] (brief crosstalk)

[16:22] Eric Huang: One more thing—tool calling. We don’t do tools, but we do “JSON mode.” Some providers call it structured outputs. Does quantization tend to break that?

[16:34] Jonas Weber: It can. Especially for “tight” formatting tasks. That’s why we recommend strict validators and route-level controls. In many cases int8 is okay; int4 is more likely to introduce small deviations.

[16:49] Mateo Alvarez: Also, temperature matters. If you run with low temperature, you usually get more stable formatting.

[16:55] Sofia Reyes: We run low temp already.

[16:58] Nina Patel: For batch summaries, we can even go deterministic.

[17:02] Jonas Weber: Great.

[17:05] Markus Klein: Let’s align on what we need from you to kick off:
1) Two routes, traffic volume estimates.
2) Prompt sets and expected output requirements.
3) Baseline metrics—current cost per million tokens, p95 latency, and error rates.
4) Any constraints on region/hardware.

[17:26] Nina Patel: We can provide 1–3. For 4, we don’t know hardware because it’s hosted. We care about US-East region.

[17:35] Markus Klein: That’s fine. We’ll map to what we run there and ensure compatibility.

[17:41] Mateo Alvarez: If we need Dedicated for stable measurements, we’ll tell you, but we can likely do it in Hosted.

[17:48] Eric Huang: What about pricing for Dedicated? Not today, but soon.

[17:52] Markus Klein: Yep, separate conversation. For POC we’ll keep it simple.

[18:00] Aditya Rao: Another detail: route-level toggles can include a “max canary %” and “auto-disable on regression.” For POC, we can set “never exceed 25% unless explicitly approved.”

[18:14] Nina Patel: I like that.

[18:16] Sofia Reyes: Same.

[18:18] Markus Klein: Any other concerns?

[18:21] Eric Huang: Observability. Can we see, per request, whether it hit quantized path?

[18:27] Mateo Alvarez: Yes, in traces. Also aggregated metrics. You can also get headers back in some setups, but usually it’s in the console.

[18:37] Nina Patel: We’d want it in metrics, not per-request headers.

[18:41] Mateo Alvarez: Understood.

[18:43] Jonas Weber: And we’ll attach offline eval results to the profile version we propose. So you have a paper trail.

[18:52] Nina Patel: Great.

[19:00] (time jump; discussion continues on specifics, some repeated)

[27:14] Sofia Reyes: Just to confirm: if we enable quantization on “batch summarize,” and we see a validity drop or quality dip, we can disable and everything goes back to baseline without redeploying.

[27:26] Aditya Rao: Correct.

[27:27] Markus Klein: And we’ll define exactly what metrics trigger rollback so you don’t have to “feel it out.”

[27:36] Nina Patel: Perfect.

[33:08] Eric Huang: Are there cases where quantization changes tokenization or token counts? Because our billing model is token-based.

[33:16] Aditya Rao: Tokenization should be identical; you’re running the same model family. But cost attribution can show different compute cost even if tokens are the same.

[33:26] Markus Klein: For your internal cost, we’ll measure $/1M tokens and $/doc.

[39:55] Nina Patel: Okay, I think we’re aligned. What’s the next step on your side?

[40:00] Markus Klein: I’ll send a short POC plan doc by Thursday with proposed routes, canary plan, and success metrics. Jonas will propose eval thresholds and what we need from your prompt sets. Mateo will confirm which profile(s) we recommend first.

[40:18] Jonas Weber: And if you can share sample outputs and what “good” looks like for batch summaries, that helps. Like length constraints, must-include fields.

[40:27] Sofia Reyes: Yep, we can do that.

[40:30] Eric Huang: And we’ll send the JSON schema. It’s pretty strict.

[40:35] Markus Klein: Perfect.

[40:38] Nina Patel: Can we schedule a follow up next week? Same group, plus maybe our security person if needed.

[40:46] Markus Klein: Yeah. Let’s do a technical deep dive focusing on JSON-mode stability and rollback signals.

[40:55] Aditya Rao: Works for me.

[41:00] Markus Klein: Cool. Anything else before we drop?

[41:04] Nina Patel: Just reiterating: cost is the driver. If we can’t see meaningful savings, we won’t move.

[41:10] Markus Klein: Totally fair. We’ll set expectations up front and we’ll be transparent if a given model/profile isn’t a good fit.

[41:18] (wrap-up)

Recap (verbal)
- Start POC with batch summarization route using a conservative quant profile (likely int8) and evaluate cost/latency/quality.
- Keep interactive and JSON-mode route baseline initially; optionally add JSON route canary only with strict validators + rollback.
- Define success criteria: >=30% cost reduction on batch route, stable reliability, and no meaningful quality regression.
- Next week: deep dive on format validity metrics + automatic rollback triggers.
